newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish govt signals IVO privatisation is on.
newsitem.headline: Finnish govt signals IVO privatisation is on.

text.p: The Finnish government on Tuesday signalled that the privatisation of state-owned power group Imatran Voima Oy (IVO) is definitively on, IVO communications director Antti Ruuskanen said on Tuesday.
"It's a signal that IVO is coming onto the market," Ruuskanen told Reuters by telephone.
He was referring to a statement with the government's supplementary budget that it was seeking parliament's authorisation to give up its two-thirds majority holding in IVO.
But the state will retain voting control in the company, the government added.
Ruuskanen said that was important, as it made clear to potential investors the maximum size of the slice of IVO coming up for sale.

"An asset chunk of this size is on its way ... in the next few years," he said, referring to the up to 50 percent stake of IVO the state might put up for sale. "It will certainly not be sold all in one piece," he added.

It was apparent that the ministry of trade and industry (KTM) -- the administrative arm in charge of state-controlled industrial companies -- wanted "more room to manoeuvre when planning the sale of the (IVO) shares," Ruuskanen said.

But a move towards a flotation was unlikely to take place until next year, he said, referring to earlier comments from the ministry that IVO's national grid must first be divested into a new separate national grid company.
"After the national grid issue has been settled, we can start looking at IVO's ownership base," Matti Vuoria, KTM permanent under-secretary of state, said earlier this month.
This divestment was scheduled to be completed by year-end but the timetable was tight, Ruuskanen said.

With Finnish electricity markets due to be fully liberalised from the start of 1997, it is logical for IVO to become a listed company, Ruuskanen said. The company last year joined a state-sponsored domestic road show aimed at private investors.
IVO was already making "internal preparations" for a listing, Ruuskanen added, but noted it is up to the state to decide when and how to start the process.

In 1995, IVO's profit before extraordinary items rose to 1.13 billion markka from 347 million and EPS improved to 7.28 markka from 2.49 markka, while net sales rose to 8.06 billion markka from 7.60 billion.
It raised its dividend to 1.50 markka from 1.20 markka.
The state directly owns around 95 percent of Imatran Voima and the government social insurance institution holds the remainder, in effect giving the state full ownership of the company.
